Code for all the analyses are available at: https://github.com/dbrookswr/Probes/blob/main/ProbeGHQs1.Rnw, using knitr [18]. Thus, the data are available and the code can be replicated providing the person has the freeware LaTeX and R, and the associated packages.

Recent innovations in survey methods may increase the likelihood that satisificing, as opposed to optimizing, occurs. An increasingly common method to recruit participants is to use companies like MTurk (www.mturk.com/) and Prolific (www.prolific.com/) to sample people from their lists of those willing to do tasks for small financial incentives. This is often referred to as online crowd sourcing. Messages are sent to thousands of people and the first people to respond are included in the sample. Researchers can specify filters on those who are initially approached. Some are basic demographic filters (e.g., here just people in the US are sampled), but others are based on the person’s performance on previous surveys, for example their percentage of satisfactory ratings on previous surveys. This can lead to a kind of professional participant as these tasks are always available. This could mean that some of those responding may answer in a manner so that their task is shorter than if they responded in a different way, increasing their hourly pay rate, but in a manner that allows them to get a satisfactory rating because researchers can limit who sees their studies to those with high proportions of satisfactory ratings. The prediction is that when follow-up probes are conditional on how a person answers and that when the probes are offered is predictable, people more often will respond so that they do not receive the follow-up probes.

Predicting participants’ binary responses will be done with a binary multilevel logistic regression [14,15], with the responses nested within both participants and items, using the lme4 package [16] within R [17]. Random effects will be included for the intercept for both participants and items. A main effect for the item order, from 1–12, will be added to the model. The main effect of condition will be added to evaluate the first prediction. Next, the interaction between item order and condition will be added to evaluate the second prediction. Details of this are included in a pre-registration, published at: https://osf.io/5uf72/overview.

Ethical approval was obtained from the Office of Research Integrity – Research Protections (ORI-RP) at UNLV. They ruled that this project (UNLV-2026–110) exempt on April 21, 2026. The preregistration is at: https://osf.io/5uf72/overview. The survey is available at: https://unlv.co1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_dnhhX1HALYpRnJI.

The data are stored, time-locked, at: https://github.com/dbrookswr/Probes/commit/56b5e0b2c63effd4bfb642ecb81c31c8d680602a. The title of the file is: probesDeIdentified,csv. Code for all the analyses are available at: https://github.com/dbrookswr/Probes/blob/main/ProbeGHQs1.Rnw, using knitr [18]. Thus, the data are available and the code can be replicated providing the person has the freeware LaTeX and R, and the associated packages.

Psychological scales are the foundation of much social and medical scientific research and are also used by practitioners when evaluating clients in these fields. A typical scale might ask a series of questions where the participant has to choose a single response alternative to summarize their belief. Asking a follow probe could help to check that the participant is interpreting the item as intended and as such help to evaluate the validity of the responses [1]. The follow-up probe can allow the participant to describe their belief in more detail than afforded with a closed forced choice response. Practitioners often use scales, particularly short forms of scales, with their clients as a screening device to help them decide if further diagnostic tests should be done [2]. Consider a practitioner asking the following item from the General Health Questionnaire (GHQ-12) [for a meta-analysis of this form, see 3]: “Felt capable of making decisions about things?”, and that they were offered these two response options: “More than usual” and “Less than usual.” Asking a person who responds “less than usual” to provide more information, like to describe an example, could help the practitioner decide how concerned they should be.

Follow-up probes are routinely used when constructing scales to make sure participants are interpreting the items correctly [4]. If used with an existing scale a key question, and the one asked in this study, is whether this affects participants’ responses to these questions. To address this question, it is useful to consider the cognitive aspects of survey responding [5–7]. Humans do not always seek optimal solutions to their tasks, but instead provide satisfactory solutions [8]. This satisficing has been observed in different types of surveys [9].

The General Health Questionnaire (GHQ) [10] is the scale used in this study. This was chosen because it is a popular scale used by both researchers and practitioners across the health, medical, and social sciences. The GHQ comes in several formats, with different numbers of items and different response alternative sets. Here the GHQ-12 (12 items) with binary response format is used. The items describe a psychological experience like “Felt capable of making decisions about things?” and participants say whether they are experiencing this more or less than usual. Here, if the person says less than usual, this may suggest a psychological concern. A recent meta-analysis of several studies using the GHQ-12 shows good reliability [3], though questions have been raised about combining items that require reverse scoring with other items [11], an issue that has also been raised for other scales [12,13].

Table 1 shows the proportion replying with the psychologically concerning response in the two conditions. The proportions for each of the trial orders, 1–12, are higher for the control condition than those offered a probe when giving the psychologically concerning response, as consistent with prediction #1. Given the sample size the width the 95% confidence intervals are approximately .08. The Wilson interval was used as recommended in Agresti [19]. Summing the number of psychologically concerning responses for all individuals, the mean for the control condition was 5.17 (sd = 4.23) and the mean for the probe condition was 3.26 (sd = 3.22). This difference is approximately d = 0.51 standard deviations.

The main inferential method for evaluating the two main predictions is a multilevel logistic regression [14,15] predicting whether the concerning response was given, allowing the intercept to vary by both the item and the person. The item order as a numeric variable was added, and then the experimental condition added. This evaluates the first prediction. Table 2 shows this improves the prediction (i.e., AIC and BIC lower than the previous run, p-value associated with the difference in models near zero). The 95% confidence interval for this effect was (−1.40, −0.82). The point estimate was β = −1.11.

The interaction between item order and the experimental condition was added to the model to evaluate the second prediction, that the difference between the probe and the control conditions increased during the duration of the scale. Table 2 shows this was observed (i.e., AIC and BIC lower the previous model, p-value associated with the difference in models near zero). The 95% bootstrap confidence interval [20,21] for this effect was (−0.17, −0.11). The point estimate was β = −0.14. Figure 1 shows both the predicted effects for the probability of giving the psychologically concerning response. As the scale continues, the probability of those giving the psychologically concerning approaches zero.

The total time to complete the survey within Qualtrics was recorded as well as the time spent on each binary item of the GHQ-12. The total time is a proxy variable for the cost of the survey. The time taken with online surveys is usually positively skewed. Here the total time had a skewness of 5.33. With positively skewed data analysts often work with the geometric mean rather than the arithmetic mean. However, this should depend on the research question [22]. Here the question is framed about the total cost and therefore the arithmetic mean will be used. The mean time for the control group was 2.96 minutes (sd = 2.11) and for the probe group was 7.21 minutes (sd = 6.53). This means, on average, the control group were paid more than twice as much per hour than the probe group. The data are skewed and heteroskedastic so a bootstrap t-test was used [23] and confirmed the control group had a lower mean. The 95% confidence interval was (−4.84, −3.65) fewer minutes in the control condition, with an associated p < .001.

The individual binary item times are a way of estimating the number of mental tasks performed [24]. In the preregistration these analyses were described as exploratory and the predicted direction was not stated. Here the interest is whether there was a multiplicative shift in time duration, so the geometric means and geometric standard deviations are reported. Further explorations were done including looking at whether item response times varied during the scale administration. Beginning with the model with the interaction (and their main effects) of experimental condition and whether the psychological concerning response was given, the item order (1–12) was added to the model and improved the fit: ∆χ2(1) = 9.04, p = .003. Adding the interaction between order and either the experimental condition (∆χ2(1) = 27.43, p < .001) or their response (∆χ2(1) = 27.43, p < .001) improved the fit. The three-way interaction was also significant: ∆χ2(1) = 8.56, p = .003. Fig 2 shows the predicted geometric means for the conditions by the item order. The largest effect is the overall decrease in response time over time, and this decrease is largest for those in the probe condition who provided the psychological concerning response. Following Spiegelhalter [25], because these are exploratory analyses they will not be discussed further.

Simon’s (1956) work on people and organizations not using optimal strategies was ground-breaking in behavioral economics. Krosnick [9] showed that participants in surveys also do not use the optimal strategies to answer the survey items correctly. Here, it can be argued the expected “correct” response proportions for the binary GHQ-12 items for the probe condition should similar to the proportions in the control condition as random assignment was used to allocate people into conditions. One possibility is that not all of those in the probe condition were using a strategy to optimize performance on the task of answering these items correctly. For some it may be that their strategy was more aligned with finishing the task rapidly while still answering in a manner that appears conscientious, but with less concern about being correct. In this sense, they were optimizing but for a different goal. Answering probes that require free response take time to respond to and survey designers should consider this cost in relation to the amount of information gained [26]. In addition, Luebker et al. [27] and Hadler [28] found including probes increased the number of people who quit the survey (i.e., break offs).

There are other possibilities. One possibility is that having thought about a psychological concerning episode in response to a previous item that their retrieval of psychological concerning episode to a new prompt could be hampered [29]. Another possibility is that taking part in previous probes affects the threshold the respondent uses to believe they should give the psychological concerning responses. Research on behavioral frequency questions shows that the threshold can be changed by aspects of the question (e.g., the response alternatives) for vaguely defined events like being annoyed [30]. All the events described in the GHQ-12 (e.g., “under strain”, “feeling unhappy”) are vague descriptions. Another possibility is that taking part in the probes makes respondents think more about the items rather than just quickly providing one of the two responses. The data reported here do not directly address which of these, or others, accounts for the results.

This experiment used a popular method for conducting psychological research, online crowd sourcing platforms, that many report can produce high quality data [e.g., 31–34]. Prolific was chosen as this platform has been shown to perform well compared with these other platforms [35]. This research shows that caution should be urged if the study has an easily recognized way to make the task take less time while still performing in a manner that would appear satisfactory. It would be worth exploring if the current findings generalize to other administrative modes [see [36], for discussion of differences in survey effects by administrative mode]. Satisficing occurs in other administrative modes [9], but the size of effects may differ. It may be that using fewer probes or making them not dependent on responses (e.g., having probes also for the non-psychologically concerning response if using this with the GHQ) could lessen effects. More research is necessary also to understand if the effects generalize to more well-defined events, like whether you ate an apple that day on a food survey or have been hospitalized, and to other forms of the GHQ.
